How can a waterjet cutter improve your machining speed and accuracy? Advantages of Waterjet Cutting Future Developments and Trends Conclusion How does CNC waterjet cutting operate and what does it entail? CNC waterjet cutting is a machining technique that uses a high-pressure stream of water combined with abrasive particles to accurately cut through diverse materials. The required shape or pattern is digitally modeled and then turned into a CNC program with the use of computer numerical control (CNC) technology. An intensifier, a cutting head assembly, and a high-pressure pump are all included with the CNC waterjet cutting machine. Although the cutting head assembly is moved by the CNC system, the water jet that is guided by the nozzle erodes the material. This technique is appropriate for a variety of applications because it offers great precision, low material waste, and the capacity to cut a broad range of materials. How can a waterjet cutter improve your machining speed and accuracy? In comparison to traditional machining procedures, a waterjet cutter improves machining speed and precision significantly. The fact that it cuts without making contact is one of its primary advantages. Since the cutting tool and the material are not in direct touch, there is no wear or damage to the tool, guaranteeing accurate and constant cutting performance throughout time. Waterjet cutters can attain high cutting speeds, particularly when abrasive particles are added to the waterjet stream. By efficiently eroding the material, the high-velocity waterjet facilitates faster cutting than with traditional machining techniques. Shorter production cycles and greater productivity are the results of this faster production. To further enhance precision multi-axis movement, waterjet cutters come with sophisticated CNC control systems installed. Due to its adaptability, precise and detailed cuts can be produced by using sophisticated and intricate cutting patterns. The CNC system accurately controlled the cutting head's movement, guaranteeing accurate results even with intricate geometries. The capacity of waterjet cutting to retain material characteristics and dimensional precision is an additional benefit. It doesn't produce heat during cutting because it's a cold-cutting procedure. This ensures that the finished product fulfills the required criteria by removing the possibility of thermal deformation or heat-affected zones in the material. In addition, the kerf width of waterjet cutters is relatively thin, usually between 0.1 and 0.3 millimeters. This narrow-cut size reduces material waste, enabling effective material utilization and lowering total production costs. Lastly, various materials, including metals, composites, stone, glass, polymers, and more, maybe cut through by waterjet cutters due to their extreme versatility. Because of its adaptability, waterjet cutting can be used in a wide range of sectors and industries, including the architectural, and creative industries. In summary, waterjet cutters are an effective tool for increasing machining speed and precision in several production processes because of their non-contact cutting, fast cutting speeds, precise multi-axis control, dimensional accuracy, tiny kerf width, and material diversity. Advantages of Waterjet Cutting With so many benefits, waterjet cutting is a popular cutting technique throughout an extensive variety of sectors. Its adaptability is one of its main benefits. Metals, stone, glass, polymers, composites, and many more materials may all be cut through with ease with waterjet cutting. The cold cutting technique of waterjet cutting is very beneficial since it produces no heat when cutting. Besides preventing material distortion, warping, or changes in material properties, this also prevents the creation of heat-affected zones (HAZ). Particularly useful for heat-sensitive materials are plastics and some metals. Another benefit is that the workpiece is subjected to very little mechanical stress during waterjet cutting. The non-contact cutting technique and the lack of mechanical forces reduce the possibility of material deformation or structural damage. Because of this, waterjet cutting is appropriate for materials that are brittle or sensitive and could be distorted or broken by other cutting techniques. Future Developments and Trends Waterjet cutting is set to undergo significant advancements and transformative trends in the coming years. Researchers and manufacturers are actively working towards increasing cutting speeds through technological innovations in pump systems, nozzle design, and abrasive delivery mechanisms. Precision and accuracy will be further enhanced by leveraging advancements in CNC control systems and motion control technologies, enabling intricate and complex cuts with tighter tolerances. Automation will play a larger role in waterjet cutting, with the integration of robotics for material loading and unloading, as well as seamless integration with other manufacturing processes to create efficient production lines. The utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms will optimize cutting parameters, predict tool wear, and improve overall cutting strategies. Multi-axis cutting capabilities will continue to advance, enabling waterjet systems to effortlessly navigate three-dimensional contours and shapes. Furthermore, the industry's focus on sustainability will drive efforts to minimize water consumption, reduce abrasive waste, and explore eco-friendly abrasive materials. Waterjet cutting will also find synergy with additive manufacturing processes, such as 3D printing, for post-processing tasks like support structure removal and precise finishing. These future developments and trends will shape waterjet cutting as an indispensable and versatile cutting method in various industries, offering increased speed, precision, automation, and environmental sustainability. Conclusion In conclusion, waterjet cutting offers numerous advantages in terms of machining speed and accuracy. Its non-contact cutting nature, high cutting speeds, multi-axis capabilities, minimal material distortion, narrow kerf width, and versatility with various materials make it a powerful tool for improving productivity and precision in manufacturing processes. Additionally, future developments and trends in waterjet cutting, such as increased cutting speeds, improved precision, enhanced automation, integration of AI and machine learning, eco-friendly solutions, and integration with additive manufacturing, promise even greater advancements and opportunities for the industry. As technology continues to evolve, waterjet cutting will remain a valuable and versatile cutting method for industries seeking efficient and accurate material processing. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Three Types of EDM Machining and How They Differ Published Jan 11, 2024, updated Aug 21, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining Materials and Applications in EDM Machining Differences between these three techniques Conclusion What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining EDM, or Electrical Discharge Machining, serves as a substitute for traditional machining methods when dealing with tough materials, particularly refractory metals and intricate shapes that are challenging to cut. Wire EDM enables the attainment of precision cuts with tolerances that would otherwise be unachievable, while hole drilling EDM excels in achieving precise diameters and roundness. Overall, EDM ensures exceptional precision and exceptionally low Ra levels, resulting in high-quality surface finishes. This characteristic reduces the need for extensive post-processing, ultimately lowering costs associated with manufacturing components that are notoriously difficult to produce. Technique 1: Hole Drilling EDM Hole Drilling EDM, also known as EDM Hole Drilling or EDM Micro-Drilling, is a specialized variant of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM). We specifically designed it to create precise and accurate holes in various materials, including metals and alloys. In Hole Drilling EDM, a small-diameter electrode, typically a rotating brass or copper tube, is used to generate a series of rapid electrical discharges. These discharges occur between the electrode and the workpiece, creating controlled erosion and gradually drilling a hole through the material. The process involves flushing a dielectric fluid, such as deionized water, through the electrode to flush away debris and cool the workpiece. The dielectric fluid also acts as a conductor for the electrical discharges. We value hole Drilling EDM for its ability to create highly accurate holes with tight tolerances, even in materials that are difficult to machine using conventional drilling methods. It is commonly used in industries such as aerospace, medical, automotive, and electronics, where precision holes are required for applications like cooling channels, fuel injection nozzles, or turbine blades. Technique 2: Sinker Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a type of procedure used for shaping and machining conductive materials. We refer it to as sinker discharge machining, sinker EDM, or conventional EDM. In Sinker Discharge Machining, a tool called a "sinker electrode" is used, which is typically made of graphite or copper. It shaped the sinker electrode to match the desired form or cavity that needs to be created in the workpiece. The process involves placing the sinker electrode close to the workpiece, with a dielectric fluid, such as oil or deionized water, acting as a medium between them. A series of electrical discharges, or sparks, are generated between the sinker electrode and the workpiece. These electrical discharges create controlled erosion, gradually removing material from the workpiece and shaping it according to the geometry of the sinker electrode. Sinker Release Intricate and complicated forms, such as molds, dies, and tooling components, are frequently made using machining. Because it does not need mechanical effort and doesn't create any noticeable heat-affected zones, it works especially well for cutting tough materials. Sinker EDM is capable of high accuracy and precise surface finishes, making it suited for sectors such as aerospace, automotive, tool and die manufacture, and medical device manufacturing. Technique 3: Wire Cut EDM Wire Cut EDM, also known as Wire Electrical Discharge Machining or Wire EDM, is a specialized kind of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) used for the precision cutting and shaping of conductive materials. A sequence of electrical discharges, or sparks, between the wire and the workpiece, are produced throughout the operation. The substance melts and evaporates because of the controlled erosion produced by these electrical discharges. The wire advances continuously, guaranteeing a continuous cutting action and enabling the machining of intricate forms and curves. Tight tolerances may be achieved, and wire-cut EDM is highly accurate. Cutting complex forms, thin sections, and contours in a variety of materials, such as metals, alloys, and conductive ceramics, is a popular use for it. Producing dies, molds, and tooling components for the precise engineering, automotive, aerospace, and electronics sectors is very helpful. Wire Cut EDM offers advantages, such as the ability to cut materials regardless of their hardness, minimal heat-affected zones, and the ability to achieve fine surface finishes. It is a flexible machining technique that allows for the high repeatability manufacturing of intricate and accurate components. Materials and Applications in EDM Machining EDM primarily handles materials that pose challenges for conventional machining methods, including tungsten, molybdenum, and hardened tool steels. Additionally, materials like titanium and austenitic stainless steels, which demonstrate significant work hardening during mechanical machining processes, are well-suited for EDM. As these materials harden while being machined, they become increasingly difficult to cut. Consequently, this hardening phenomenon often leads to a reduction in the accuracy of the machined part features. Electric discharge machining finds application in the production of molds for plastic injection molding and metal die casting. It is utilized to create intricate cavities in pre-hardened materials, showcasing its proficiency in achieving precise and complex cavity shapes, as well as executing deep cuts. Industries such as aerospace, automobile, and electronics also rely on EDM for fabricating prototypes and manufacturing various components. Differences between these three techniques Different types of EDM are classified based on their operations and applications. One example is wire EDM, which utilizes a linear feed wire electrode to make primarily two-dimensional cuts. We position the electrode wire on a guide made of diamond or sapphire, and the dielectric fluid used is typically deionized water. Brass or galvanized brass is commonly employed for the electrode material. In contrast, sinker discharge EDM allows for the utilization of intricate electrode shapes to create equally complex cavities. Graphite or copper electrodes are pre-machined into the desired shape and then eroded into the workpiece, resulting in holes that mirror the shape of the electrode. Drilling EDM is capable of producing smaller and deeper holes compared to traditional drilling methods. This enables precise diameters, roundness, excellent surface finishes, and eliminates burrs. Wire EDM enables the attainment of precision cuts with tolerances that would otherwise be unachievable, while hole drilling EDM excels in achieving precise diameters and roundness. Overall, EDM ensures exceptional precision and exceptionally low Ra levels, resulting in high-quality surface finishes. This characteristic reduces the need for extensive post-processing, ultimately lowering costs associated with manufacturing components that are notoriously difficult to produce. Technique 1: Hole Drilling EDM Hole Drilling EDM, also known as EDM Hole Drilling or EDM Micro-Drilling, is a specialized variant of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM). We specifically designed it to create precise and accurate holes in various materials, including metals and alloys. In Hole Drilling EDM, a small-diameter electrode, typically a rotating brass or copper tube, is used to generate a series of rapid electrical discharges. These discharges occur between the electrode and the workpiece, creating controlled erosion and gradually drilling a hole through the material. The process involves flushing a dielectric fluid, such as deionized water, through the electrode to flush away debris and cool the workpiece. The dielectric fluid also acts as a conductor for the electrical discharges. We value hole Drilling EDM for its ability to create highly accurate holes with tight tolerances, even in materials that are difficult to machine using conventional drilling methods. It is commonly used in industries such as aerospace, medical, automotive, and electronics, where precision holes are required for applications like cooling channels, fuel injection nozzles, or turbine blades. Technique 2: Sinker Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a type of procedure used for shaping and machining conductive materials. We refer it to as sinker discharge machining, sinker EDM, or conventional EDM. In Sinker Discharge Machining, a tool called a "sinker electrode" is used, which is typically made of graphite or copper. It shaped the sinker electrode to match the desired form or cavity that needs to be created in the workpiece. The process involves placing the sinker electrode close to the workpiece, with a dielectric fluid, such as oil or deionized water, acting as a medium between them. Technique 3: Wire Cut EDM Wire Cut EDM, also known as Wire Electrical Discharge Machining or Wire EDM, is a specialized kind of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) used for the precision cutting and shaping of conductive materials. A sequence of electrical discharges, or sparks, between the wire and the workpiece, are produced throughout the operation. The substance melts and evaporates because of the controlled erosion produced by these electrical discharges. The wire advances continuously, guaranteeing a continuous cutting action and enabling the machining of intricate forms and curves. Tight tolerances may be achieved, and wire-cut EDM is highly accurate. Cutting complex forms, thin sections, and contours in a variety of materials, such as metals, alloys, and conductive ceramics, is a popular use for it. It is a flexible machining technique that allows for the high repeatability manufacturing of intricate and accurate components. Additionally, materials like titanium and austenitic stainless steels, which demonstrate significant work hardening during mechanical machining processes, are well-suited for EDM. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals How EDM Wire Cutting Works: Complete Guide to Precision CNC Wire Cutting Published Jul 20, 2025, updated Dec 23, 2025 5 min Cutting Metal with Electricity? If you’re in the world of high-precision manufacturing, chances are you’ve heard of EDM wire cutting , short for Electrical Discharge Machining (Wire EDM) . It’s not your typical metal cutting method. There are no spinning blades, drills, or end mills. Instead, it slices through metal with electrical sparks , offering unmatched precision and control. But how does EDM wire cutting work ? What makes it so popular in aerospace, mold-making, and medical device industries? And where does it fit compared to traditional CNC cutting methods? Let’s answer all these questions. What Is Wire EDM Cutting? Wire EDM cutting , or simply wire cutting , is a type of electrical discharge machining that uses a thin wire as the electrode to erode material from a conductive workpiece. Instead of physical contact, it relies on high-voltage electrical discharges (sparks) to cut intricate shapes and tight tolerances, often as fine as ±0.001mm. Despite how clean it looks, it’s actually controlled erosion at a microscopic level . That’s what gives it incredible accuracy. How Wire EDM Works: The Process Explained To understand how wire EDM works , imagine slicing butter with a hot wire, except in this case, you're cutting hardened steel without any contact. Here’s how it works, step by step: 1. Setup : A copper or brass wire (usually 0.1–0.3mm thick) is threaded through the machine and guided by diamond guides. 2. Workpiece Placement : The part to be cut is submerged in deionized water , which cools the area and flushes away debris. 3. Electrical Discharge : A high-frequency spark jumps from the wire to the workpiece, removing tiny bits of metal in rapid succession. 4. CNC Control : Like other CNC machines, G-code controls the wire path, making it ideal for complex contours and internal cuts. 5. Wire Movement : The wire moves continuously from a supply spool, so fresh electrode is always available, improving cut quality and avoiding contamination. Benefits of EDM Wire Cutting EDM wire cutting isn’t just flashy, it has real, measurable benefits: ● No Mechanical Force : Since there’s no physical contact, you don’t stress or deform the material. ● Incredible Precision : Tolerances as tight as ±0.001mm are possible, great for injection molds, dies, and medical tools. ● Material Hardness Doesn’t Matter : You can cut hardened steel, titanium, Inconel , or any conductive material, regardless of hardness. ● Complex Geometry : Need sharp internal corners or intricate contours? EDM wire machines excel at them. ● Clean Finish : Cuts are smooth and burr-free, often requiring little or no post-processing. While wire EDM excels in intricate and conductive material cutting, it’s worth exploring how it compares to other methods like laser vs waterjet cutting, each with its own precision, speed, and material compatibility. Limitations of EDM Wire Machines Like all technologies, EDM wire machines aren’t perfect for everything: ● Slow Compared to Milling : It’s precise, but not fast. CNC milling may be more efficient for roughing. ● Conductive Materials Only : Non-conductive materials like plastic, wood, or glass can’t be cut using EDM. ● Higher Operational Costs : Wire spools, deionized water systems, and power consumption add up. Where CNC Wire Cutting Machines Shine EDM wire cutting is often chosen for high-value, low-tolerance parts where traditional machining falls short. Some industries where CNC wire cutting machines are essential include: ● Tool and Die Making : For punches, molds, and dies with internal details. ● Aerospace : Precision turbine blades, fuel system parts, and sensor components. ● Medical : Surgical tools, implants, and orthodontic hardware. ● Electronics : Micro-components, connectors, and cavities in complex housings. CNC vs EDM: What's the Difference? Though EDM wire machines are part of the CNC family, they differ significantly from traditional subtractive CNC machines: Feature CNC Milling Wire EDM Cutting Contact Method Physical cutting Electrical erosion Material Limit Most materials Only conductive materials Precision High Ultra-high Tool Wear Yes None (constant wire feed) Internal Corners Rounded (cutter radius) Sharp (0° radius possible) Surface Finish May need finishing Often smooth & burr-free Need high-precision parts without worrying about tooling stress or surface imperfections? Our machining services are ideal for prototypes and functional parts requiring tight tolerances and clean finishes . Get a quote here Why Wire EDM Still Matters Even with laser cutting, 5-axis machining, and waterjet options, EDM wire cutting remains irreplaceable for certain jobs. If you’re working with tight tolerance parts in hardened steel , no other process offers this level of detail and repeatability. So, Is EDM Wire Cutting Right for Your Project? If you're wondering "what is wire cutting EDM really used for?" , the answer is simple: uncompromising precision in hard-to-machine materials . Whether you're building molds, aerospace components, or detailed electrical parts, EDM wire cutting offers unparalleled accuracy and finish. If your part tolerances are tight and your material is conductive, this might just be the perfect solution. Benefits of EDM Wire Cutting EDM wire cutting isn’t just flashy, it has real, measurable benefits: ● No Mechanical Force : Since there’s no physical contact, you don’t stress or deform the material. ● Incredible Precision : Tolerances as tight as ±0.001mm are possible, great for injection molds, dies, and medical tools. ● Material Hardness Doesn’t Matter : You can cut hardened steel, titanium, Inconel , or any conductive material, regardless of hardness. ● Complex Geometry : Need sharp internal corners or intricate contours? EDM wire machines excel at them. ● Clean Finish : Cuts are smooth and burr-free, often requiring little or no post-processing. Limitations of EDM Wire Machines Like all technologies, EDM wire machines aren’t perfect for everything: ● Slow Compared to Milling : It’s precise, but not fast. CNC milling may be more efficient for roughing. ● Conductive Materials Only : Non-conductive materials like plastic, wood, or glass can’t be cut using EDM. ● Higher Operational Costs : Wire spools, deionized water systems, and power consumption add up. If you’re working with tight tolerance parts in hardened steel , no other process offers this level of detail and repeatability. So, Is EDM Wire Cutting Right for Your Project? If you're wondering "what is wire cutting EDM really used for?" , the answer is simple: uncompromising precision in hard-to-machine materials . Whether you're building molds, aerospace components, or detailed electrical parts, EDM wire cutting offers unparalleled accuracy and finish. If your part tolerances are tight and your material is conductive, this might just be the perfect solution. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals High-Speed CNC Machining: What It Is and When to Use It Published Jul 04, 2025, updated Jul 30, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What Is High-Speed CNC Machining, Really? What Makes High-Speed Machining Possible? When to Use High-Speed CNC Machining When NOT to Use High-Speed Machining HSC vs. Traditional CNC: A Summary Industry Examples of HSC in Action Conclusion: Speed Is a Tool, Not a Shortcut In the world of precision manufacturing, speed isn't just about working faster—it's about working smarter. High-speed CNC machining (HSC) is often misunderstood as simply “spinning the spindle faster,” but in practice, it's a sophisticated, multi-variable strategy that blends tooling, motion control, thermal dynamics, and material science. For engineers, machinists, and manufacturers dealing with complex geometries, tight tolerances, and short lead times, high-speed machining isn’t a trend—it’s a competitive advantage. This article explores what HSC really is, how it differs from traditional methods, when it's worth using, and when it's not. (pexels) What Is High-Speed CNC Machining, Really? There’s no universal speed threshold that defines HSC, but in practical terms, it refers to machining processes that operate at: High spindle speeds : typically 15,000 to 60,000 RPM High feed rates : over 10 m/min, sometimes exceeding 30 m/min Low depth-of-cut with high material removal rates Optimized tool paths : using adaptive or trochoidal milling strategies Minimized cutting forces : preserving tool and machine integrity But the speed itself isn’t the defining factor— it’s the system’s ability to maintain stability and accuracy at those speeds . It’s Not Just Faster. It’s Fundamentally Different. Where traditional CNC milling relies on deeper, heavier cuts at lower speeds and forces, high-speed machining uses lighter, faster passes —reducing heat buildup, tool deflection, and mechanical stress. This results in smoother finishes, tighter tolerances, and in many cases, a shorter overall cycle time despite the “lighter” passes. What Makes High-Speed Machining Possible? To achieve HSC, you need more than just a high-RPM spindle. The entire machine system—hardware, software, tooling, and fixturing—needs to be designed or upgraded for high-speed operation: 1. Machine Tool Construction Stiff yet lightweight structures : minimize vibration and thermal distortion High-acceleration linear guides and ball screws : for rapid tool positioning Advanced control systems : with look-ahead features, dynamic path optimization, and jerk control 2. Spindle Technology High-speed spindles with minimal runout : critical for maintaining balance at high RPMs Oil-air or hybrid ceramic bearings : to handle thermal loads Integrated cooling : to stabilize performance over long runs 3. Tooling & Workholding Balanced, high-flute-count end mills : optimized for chip evacuation and lower force Heat-resistant coatings : like DLC or TiAlN for longevity Precision holders : such as shrink-fit or hydraulic chucks for minimal runout 4. CAM and Toolpath Strategy High-speed machining shines when paired with intelligent toolpaths such as: Adaptive clearing Trochoidal milling Constant engagement strategies These help maintain consistent cutting forces and prevent sudden tool load spikes. When to Use High-Speed CNC Machining 1. Thin-Walled or Delicate Parts Lightweight aerospace brackets and even medical housings often require minimal vibration and tight tolerances. HSC enables: Reduced tool deflection Low cutting forces that prevent wall distortion Minimal finishing post-processes 2. Hard Materials or Hardened Tool Steels For mold & die applications or cutting materials like Inconel, hardened steel, or titanium, high-speed machining with optimized tooling can: Prevent work hardening Improve surface finish Eliminate secondary operations (like EDM or polishing) 3. Aluminum and Non-Ferrous Materials Materials like 6061 and 7075 aluminum alloys respond exceptionally well to HSC, especially in high-volume applications like consumer electronics or automotive parts. You get: Mirror-like finishes High throughput Reduced burr formation 4. Complex 3D Geometries When working with sculpted surfaces—such as impellers, orthopedic implants, or molds—HSC, especially with 5-axis setups, can: Handle fine details Reduce machining time on intricate forms Improve surface quality, especially with ball-end tools 5. Prototyping and Short Lead Time Jobs High-speed setups often allow faster first part delivery , even if the roughing cycle is slightly longer. Combined with modern CAM software, you can go from CAD to chip in record time. When NOT to Use High-Speed Machining Despite its advantages, HSC isn’t always the right tool for the job. It’s best to avoid HSC when: 1. Roughing Large Steel Blocks Traditional low-RPM roughing with indexable tooling is more efficient for removing hundreds of cubic centimeters of material quickly. 2. Your Machine Can’t Handle It If your CNC has low spindle RPMs, insufficient rigidity, or outdated motion control, forcing HSC strategies can lead to: Tool chatter Premature wear Inconsistent finishes or even spindle damage 3. Cost Is a Bigger Concern Than Quality If you’re making simple brackets with loose tolerances in high quantities, the return on HSC investment may not be justified. HSC vs. Traditional CNC: A Summary Feature High-Speed CNC Traditional CNC Cutting Strategy Many light, fast passes Few heavy, slower passes Best Use Cases Precision, complex parts Bulk material removal Surface Finish Excellent Good to Fair Tool Life (with setup) Longer Shorter (under heavy load) Machine Requirements High-rigidity, advanced control Standard Learning Curve Steeper (toolpaths, setup) Moderate Cycle Time Often faster for complex parts Faster for simple roughing Industry Examples of HSC in Action ✦ Aerospace: Machining 7075 aluminum wing ribs with HSC can reduce cycle time by 30–40% and improve fatigue performance thanks to smoother edges and fewer stress concentrators. ✦ Medical: Hip implants and dental components require both biocompatible materials and flawless surface finishes—ideal for 5-axis high-speed strategies using ceramic-coated tools. ✦ Mold & Die: Direct machining of hardened tool steel with ball-nose end mills using HSC avoids lengthy EDM processes, accelerating time-to-market for injection molds. Conclusion: Speed Is a Tool, Not a Shortcut High-speed CNC machining is more than just running fast—it’s about optimizing every component in the machining system to cut more efficiently, more accurately, and with better repeatability . For engineers and manufacturing professionals, understanding when to adopt HSC—and when not to—is critical . Used properly, it’s a tool that can dramatically enhance part quality, lead time, and profitability. Misused, it’s a shortcut to broken tools and burnt-out spindles. If your work involves precision surfaces, tight tolerances, or high-mix low-volume production, HSC might be the secret weapon your process has been missing. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Advantages of Laser Cutting vs. CNC Milling for Sheet Metal Fabrication Published null, updated Mar 13, 2025 4 min In the field of sheet metal processing, laser cutting and CNC milling are two core processes known for their high precision, high efficiency and ability to process complex structures. Whether it's aerospace parts or consumer electronics housings, choosing the right processing technology has a direct impact on cost, efficiency and product quality. This article will be an in-depth comparison of laser cutting and CNC milling process advantages, analysis of its application scenarios, and provide companies with technology selection of the practical guide. I. Laser cutting: the perfect balance of speed and precision 1. Core process advantages Ultra-high precision: fibre laser cutting machine can achieve ±0.05mm tolerance (such as TruLaser 5030), smooth and burr-free cut. Wide material adaptability: support for stainless steel (0.5-30mm), aluminium alloy (0.5-25mm), copper plate (0.5-15mm) and so on. Processing efficiency: cutting speed up to 40m/min (1mm carbon steel), 3 times faster than traditional plasma cutting. 2. Typical application scenarios Thin plate precision processing: Electronic equipment shell (thickness 0.5-3mm), contour accuracy ≤ ± 0.1mm. Automotive sheet metal parts (such as door liners), cutting efficiency of 200 pieces / hour. Complex graphics processing: Artistic decorative metal screens, minimum hole diameter up to 0.2mm. 3. Cost-effectiveness analysis Case: a home appliance company processing 10,000 pieces of stainless steel panels: Laser cutting: single piece cost $ 8.5, time-consuming 3 days. Traditional stamping: mould cost $ 50,000 + single piece cost $ 6.2, the total cost is higher. II. CNC Milling: the ultimate solution for complex structures and high surface quality. 1. Core process advantages Three-dimensional machining capacity: five-axis CNC milling machine can process deep cavities, curved surfaces, shaped structures (such as impellers, mould cavities). Surface quality control: surface roughness Ra≤0.8μm after fine milling, directly achieve mirror effect. Batch consistency: Dimensional fluctuation of processing 1000 pieces of aluminium ≤ ± 0.02mm (CPK ≥ 1.67). 2. Typical application scenarios Thick plate precision parts: Aircraft engine bracket (50mm aluminium alloy), flatness ≤ 0.03mm. Hydraulic valve block (40CrMo steel), multi-hole system positional degree tolerance ± 0.01mm. Functional surface treatment: Mould insert nibble processing (VDI 3400 standard), texture depth 0.05-0.2mm. 3. Cost-effectiveness analysis Case: a medical device company processing titanium alloy joint implants: CNC milling: single piece cost $ 220, yield rate of 98%. 3D printing: single piece cost $ 380, need to follow up machining correction. III. Types of Machining Burrs Why Machining Burrs Matter Burr Removal Methods Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops Preventing Burrs in Machining Conclusion FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs CNC Machining Burrs (Envato) If you've ever run your hand across a freshly machined part and felt a sharp edge catch your skin, you've met the enemy: the burr. At first glance, it looks like a tiny flaw, but in machining, burrs are more than just a cosmetic annoyance. They can cut into assembly time, drive up costs, and in worst cases, create safety hazards for anyone handling the part. So, what is burr in machining? Think of it as the unwanted leftovers of the cutting process, those ragged edges, thin slivers, or raised ridges that show up after material is sheared, drilled, or milled. They're a headache for engineers and machinists alike because a part that isn't properly deburred can jam in an assembly, fail under stress, or even injure a technician. This is exactly why burr control matters so much in precision work. At JLCCNC, we've seen how burr-sensitive projects can make or break production runs, which is why we put the same focus on edge quality as we do on tolerances. And since our copper, steel, and aluminum machining starts at just $1 per part, even small shops can outsource tricky jobs and get parts that are both precise and safe to handle. What is Burr in Machining? (science direct) In machining, a burr is that unwanted bit of extra material left clinging to a part after a cutting process. Technically, it forms when the tool pushes or tears the material instead of slicing it away cleanly. What you get is a raised edge, a thin flap, or a tiny jagged lip that wasn't part of your CAD model, but now it's there, and it needs to be dealt with. You'll usually spot machining burrs around the usual suspects: along sharp edges, inside drilled holes, at the end of slots, or even wrapped around threads. Basically, anywhere the tool exits the cut is prime real estate for burr formation. Some are barely noticeable, while others can be sharp enough to slice a glove open or mess up an assembly fit. And here's the worst part: burrs aren't just a surface-level nuisance. They can ruin dimensional accuracy and surface quality, which is why deburring is almost always a required step in precision work. If you've read our guide on CNC Machining Surface Roughness: A Practical Guide , you'll know surface finish and edge quality often go hand in hand, burrs are just another part of that same equation. Types of Machining Burrs Not all burrs look the same, and knowing the type helps figure out the right removal method. Here's a quick breakdown of the most common machining burrs you'll run into: Burr Type Where It Shows Up What's Going On Poisson Burrs Along edges when cutting ductile metals Caused by plastic deformation pushing material sideways Roll-over Burrs Milling, drilling, and slotting operations Tool exit leaves a curled flap of material Breakout Burrs Exit side of drilled holes Material tears instead of shearing cleanly Cut-off Burrs Lathe parting or cut-off operations Extra material left behind as the tool separates the part Each of these has its own headache factor. A tiny Poisson burr might just ruin surface finish, while a chunky roll-over burr can jam an assembly or cut your hand open. Why Machining Burrs Matter (Intechopen) It's tempting to think burrs are just cosmetic, but they can cause problems way beyond looks. Here's why they matter: Impact Area How Burrs Affect It Assembly Tolerances Even a small burr can stop parts from fitting together cleanly Fatigue Life Burrs act as stress risers, shortening the lifespan of a component Safety Sharp burr edges can injure operators or end-users Post-Processing Costs Extra deburring steps = more time and money spent In high-stakes industries, one slip is all it takes. A single machining burr can cause part rejection in aerospace or medical applications, where safety margins are razor thin. And even outside of those fields, no customer wants a “finished” part that looks unfinished. Burr Removal Methods The method to remove burrs in CNC machining depends on part geometry, material, and how clean you need the finish. Here's a quick tour of the main approaches: Manual Deburring The old-school way: hand files, scrapers, sandpaper, or wire brushes. Cheap and flexible, but slow, and not consistent for production runs. Mechanical Methods Techniques like vibratory tumbling or grinding wheels are common in shops that need to batch-finish lots of smaller parts. Good for smoothing edges, but not always precise. Thermal Deburring Also called “explosive deburring.” Parts go in a sealed chamber, a gas mix is ignited, and burrs are literally burned off. Works well for internal burrs in tricky spots, but it's not the friendliest process for every material. Electrochemical Deburring This method uses an electrolyte and electric current to dissolve burrs in tight places<dynamic-value> cross-drilled holes or hydraulic components. Precise, but requires careful setup. Automated Deburring with Burr Machines This is where modern shops lean in. A burr machine uses abrasive brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to remove burrs automatically. The result: faster turnaround, less operator fatigue, and a more consistent finish. Method Pros Cons Traditional (manual / mechanical) Low entry cost, flexible for odd parts Labor intensive, inconsistent, time-consuming Automated (burr machines) High speed, repeatable results, great for production Higher upfront cost, needs proper setup Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops When people talk about shop efficiency today, burr machines and burr removal machines almost always come up. These systems combine abrasive heads, rotary tools, or even CNC attachments to take deburring from a bottleneck into a smooth step of the workflow. Machine Feature What It Does Why It Matters Abrasive Brushes Sweep away burrs on edges and surfaces Leaves a consistent finish without heavy labor Rotary Tools Target burrs in slots, grooves, or small features Great for complex part geometries CNC Integrated Deburring Toolpaths include deburring passes Saves setup time and reduces manual handling Benefits at a glance: faster cycle times, repeatable quality, and fewer operator hours spent hunched over a vise with a file. At JLCCNC , we've integrated advanced deburring directly into our workflow. That means when you send us burr-sensitive jobs, you're not just getting clean tolerances, you're getting parts that are ready to assemble straight out of the box. And with services starting at just $1/part, it's a no-brainer to let the machines (and our team) do the heavy lifting. Get a free quote today ! Preventing Burrs in Machining It's always cheaper and easier to stop burrs from forming than to spend hours removing them later. A few shop-floor best practices go a long way: Dial in tool geometry, feeds, and speeds → Sharp cutters with the right rake angle can slice cleanly instead of smearing the material. Running too slow or too shallow usually means burr city. Solid workholding → If a part vibrates or shifts even slightly, you'll see burrs at exit points. Lock it down, keep it stable. Coatings and coolants → TiN-coated tools paired with a proper cutting fluid help reduce adhesion and chip welding, both of which cause nasty edges. Design with burrs in mind → Chamfers, proper hole spacing, and avoiding thin unsupported features can dramatically reduce burr-prone zones. Conclusion Burrs might look like minor defects, but they stack up into real headaches, extra finishing costs, tolerance issues, safety risks, and sometimes full-on part rejection. The fix isn't just deburring afterward; it's knowing when to prevent burrs at the source and when to bring in the right burr machine for the cleanup. At JLCCNC , we've got both ends covered: precision machining that minimizes burr formation and automated deburring to handle the rest. The result is parts that are production-ready, safer, and more reliable. And with services starting at just $1 per component , outsourcing burr-sensitive jobs has never been simpler. FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs What is burr in machining? A burr in machining is a small, unwanted ridge or sharp edge left behind when material deforms or tears instead of cutting cleanly. How are machining burrs formed? They usually form at tool exit points<dynamic-value> hole edges, slots, or parting lines, when chips don't break away cleanly. What machine removes burrs? A burr removal machine uses brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to clean up edges quickly and consistently. Is deburring always necessary in CNC machining? Not always, but in industries like aerospace, automotive, and medical, deburring is non-negotiable for safety, fit, and reliability. What industries need strict burr control? Aerospace, medical device manufacturing, automotive, and electronics are big ones, anywhere a sharp edge or stray burr could compromise function or safety. Types of Machining Burrs Why Machining Burrs Matter Burr Removal Methods Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops Preventing Burrs in Machining Conclusion FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs CNC Machining Burrs (Envato) If you've ever run your hand across a freshly machined part and felt a sharp edge catch your skin, you've met the enemy: the burr. At first glance, it looks like a tiny flaw, but in machining, burrs are more than just a cosmetic annoyance. They can cut into assembly time, drive up costs, and in worst cases, create safety hazards for anyone handling the part. So, what is burr in machining? Think of it as the unwanted leftovers of the cutting process, those ragged edges, thin slivers, or raised ridges that show up after material is sheared, drilled, or milled. They're a headache for engineers and machinists alike because a part that isn't properly deburred can jam in an assembly, fail under stress, or even injure a technician. This is exactly why burr control matters so much in precision work. At JLCCNC, we've seen how burr-sensitive projects can make or break production runs, which is why we put the same focus on edge quality as we do on tolerances. And since our copper, steel, and aluminum machining starts at just $1 per part, even small shops can outsource tricky jobs and get parts that are both precise and safe to handle. What is Burr in Machining? (science direct) In machining, a burr is that unwanted bit of extra material left clinging to a part after a cutting process. Technically, it forms when the tool pushes or tears the material instead of slicing it away cleanly. What you get is a raised edge, a thin flap, or a tiny jagged lip that wasn't part of your CAD model, but now it's there, and it needs to be dealt with. You'll usually spot machining burrs around the usual suspects: along sharp edges, inside drilled holes, at the end of slots, or even wrapped around threads. Basically, anywhere the tool exits the cut is prime real estate for burr formation. Some are barely noticeable, while others can be sharp enough to slice a glove open or mess up an assembly fit. And here's the worst part: burrs aren't just a surface-level nuisance. They can ruin dimensional accuracy and surface quality, which is why deburring is almost always a required step in precision work. If you've read our guide on CNC Machining Surface Roughness: A Practical Guide , you'll know surface finish and edge quality often go hand in hand, burrs are just another part of that same equation. Types of Machining Burrs Not all burrs look the same, and knowing the type helps figure out the right removal method. Here's a quick breakdown of the most common machining burrs you'll run into: Burr Type Where It Shows Up What's Going On Poisson Burrs Along edges when cutting ductile metals Caused by plastic deformation pushing material sideways Roll-over Burrs Milling, drilling, and slotting operations Tool exit leaves a curled flap of material Breakout Burrs Exit side of drilled holes Material tears instead of shearing cleanly Cut-off Burrs Lathe parting or cut-off operations Extra material left behind as the tool separates the part Each of these has its own headache factor. A tiny Poisson burr might just ruin surface finish, while a chunky roll-over burr can jam an assembly or cut your hand open. Why Machining Burrs Matter (Intechopen) It's tempting to think burrs are just cosmetic, but they can cause problems way beyond looks. Here's why they matter: Impact Area How Burrs Affect It Assembly Tolerances Even a small burr can stop parts from fitting together cleanly Fatigue Life Burrs act as stress risers, shortening the lifespan of a component Safety Sharp burr edges can injure operators or end-users Post-Processing Costs Extra deburring steps = more time and money spent In high-stakes industries, one slip is all it takes. A single machining burr can cause part rejection in aerospace or medical applications, where safety margins are razor thin. And even outside of those fields, no customer wants a “finished” part that looks unfinished. Burr Removal Methods The method to remove burrs in CNC machining depends on part geometry, material, and how clean you need the finish. Here's a quick tour of the main approaches: Manual Deburring The old-school way: hand files, scrapers, sandpaper, or wire brushes. Cheap and flexible, but slow, and not consistent for production runs. Mechanical Methods Techniques like vibratory tumbling or grinding wheels are common in shops that need to batch-finish lots of smaller parts. Good for smoothing edges, but not always precise. Thermal Deburring Also called “explosive deburring.” Parts go in a sealed chamber, a gas mix is ignited, and burrs are literally burned off. Works well for internal burrs in tricky spots, but it's not the friendliest process for every material. Electrochemical Deburring This method uses an electrolyte and electric current to dissolve burrs in tight places<dynamic-value> cross-drilled holes or hydraulic components. Precise, but requires careful setup. Automated Deburring with Burr Machines This is where modern shops lean in. A burr machine uses abrasive brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to remove burrs automatically. The result: faster turnaround, less operator fatigue, and a more consistent finish. Method Pros Cons Traditional (manual / mechanical) Low entry cost, flexible for odd parts Labor intensive, inconsistent, time-consuming Automated (burr machines) High speed, repeatable results, great for production Higher upfront cost, needs proper setup Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops When people talk about shop efficiency today, burr machines and burr removal machines almost always come up. These systems combine abrasive heads, rotary tools, or even CNC attachments to take deburring from a bottleneck into a smooth step of the workflow. Machine Feature What It Does Why It Matters Abrasive Brushes Sweep away burrs on edges and surfaces Leaves a consistent finish without heavy labor Rotary Tools Target burrs in slots, grooves, or small features Great for complex part geometries CNC Integrated Deburring Toolpaths include deburring passes Saves setup time and reduces manual handling Benefits at a glance: faster cycle times, repeatable quality, and fewer operator hours spent hunched over a vise with a file. At JLCCNC , we've integrated advanced deburring directly into our workflow. That means when you send us burr-sensitive jobs, you're not just getting clean tolerances, you're getting parts that are ready to assemble straight out of the box. And with services starting at just $1/part, it's a no-brainer to let the machines (and our team) do the heavy lifting. Get a free quote today ! Preventing Burrs in Machining It's always cheaper and easier to stop burrs from forming than to spend hours removing them later. A few shop-floor best practices go a long way: Dial in tool geometry, feeds, and speeds → Sharp cutters with the right rake angle can slice cleanly instead of smearing the material. Running too slow or too shallow usually means burr city. Solid workholding → If a part vibrates or shifts even slightly, you'll see burrs at exit points. Lock it down, keep it stable. Coatings and coolants → TiN-coated tools paired with a proper cutting fluid help reduce adhesion and chip welding, both of which cause nasty edges. Design with burrs in mind → Chamfers, proper hole spacing, and avoiding thin unsupported features can dramatically reduce burr-prone zones. Conclusion Burrs might look like minor defects, but they stack up into real headaches, extra finishing costs, tolerance issues, safety risks, and sometimes full-on part rejection. The fix isn't just deburring afterward; it's knowing when to prevent burrs at the source and when to bring in the right burr machine for the cleanup. At JLCCNC , we've got both ends covered: precision machining that minimizes burr formation and automated deburring to handle the rest. The result is parts that are production-ready, safer, and more reliable. And with services starting at just $1 per component , outsourcing burr-sensitive jobs has never been simpler. FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs What is burr in machining? A burr in machining is a small, unwanted ridge or sharp edge left behind when material deforms or tears instead of cutting cleanly. How are machining burrs formed? They usually form at tool exit points<dynamic-value> hole edges, slots, or parting lines, when chips don't break away cleanly. What machine removes burrs? A burr removal machine uses brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to clean up edges quickly and consistently. Is deburring always necessary in CNC machining? Not always, but in industries like aerospace, automotive, and medical, deburring is non-negotiable for safety, fit, and reliability. What industries need strict burr control? Aerospace, medical device manufacturing, automotive, and electronics are big ones, anywhere a sharp edge or stray burr could compromise function or safety. Plastic injection molding Injection molding is the manufacturing process of injecting high-pressure thermoplastic into a mold. Ideal for high-volume production. Learn more Insert molding A manufacturing process in which a part is molded around a pre-installed insert in the tooling. Overmolding A manufacturing process in which one plastic material is molded over another to create a single component. Liquid silicone rubber molding A thermoset process that involves mixing a two-part solution together to produce flexible and durable parts. Find out more about the timeline. Download our Gantt chart. SPI surface finishes We offer any type of SPI surface finish, such as A-1, D-2 or D-3. Find the right SPI finish for your part VDI surface finishes We offer any type of VDI surface finish, such as VDI28, VDI30 or VDI 33. Looking for Mold-Tech (MT) or Yick Sang (YS) textures? We support both texture standards, along with custom surface finishes. Upload your CAD Injection molding materials Choose from a wide range of standard, engineering, and specialty materials. Additional grades are available on request. DFM & tool approval Receive extensive Design For Manufacturing analysis to approve before construction of your tool begins 4. Reorder as required You can easily reorder parts by contacting your account manager The Protolabs Network Standard - consistent quality, every time Protolabs Network applies a rigorous set of standards to every custom part, ensuring quality and consistency for injection molded components. We inspect each order dimensionally and visually during and after production. Inspection & quality documentation Advanced inspection and quality documentation are available on request, including PPAP, FAI, CMM inspection, Cpk analysis, GR&R, and IQ/OQ/PQ for qualifying projects. We have a dedicated team of injection molding project engineers and support staff on the ground to help make sure everything runs smoothly and on time, every time. "I take care of your parts from start to finish, making sure you receive the parts on time and exactly as you requested.” Shak Akharov, Injection Molding Technical Program Manager “I guarantee that your parts go through an extensive quality control process, so they will always be up to spec.” Wilmer Milloria, Quality Control Manager “I make sure we always have a manufacturing partner in our network that fits your manufacturing needs. ” Ruiqi Li, Supply Chain Manager “I ensure our customers are constantly updated on the status of the project and guarantee that they experience a smooth ordering process.” Carlos Blasco, Injection Molding Application Engineer What are the customer experiences of our injection molding service? "It was really helpful to have someone to spar with and test out new ideas on the platform, get a new price for them, and ultimately go into production.” Otect “Having someone who can be in touch with the manufacturers was essential for us.” LEKTRI.CO “You can just upload the parts and get a quote directly. It was just awesome”. Zinstax The advantages of injection molding with us Variety of materials Injection molding offers vast flexibility in material selection. Depending on the mechanical properties your parts require, you can achieve impact- and chemical-resistance, rubber-like elasticity and dimensional stability with molded parts. Our experts can help to manufacture molded parts that are optimized to perform in industrial applications, including parts designed for aerospace, automotive and consumer electronics. We can source thousands of custom materials on request and can advise you on the best choice for your project while minimizing your costs along the way. Single, multi-cavity, and family molds No matter the scale of your injection molding project, we can help you to design and build the ideal tooling and mold for cost-efficient production. As well as single molds, we can advise on multi-cavity molds that simultaneously produce multiple identical models – reducing your cost per part and speeding up production. Our manufacturing partners also work with family molds that optimize tooling costs by producing different parts within the same mold. This is ideal for parts or products that have multiple components of the same material but with different geometries. High quality standards The injection molding process results in finely tuned parts that are highly accurate and consistent. Protolabs Network guarantees the quality of every part that flows through our manufacturing partner network. Our comprehensive quality management processes ensure your molded parts are always up to spec, and that we only work with thoroughly vetted suppliers. We offer various types of quality documentation and can match your project with a manufacturing partner that has industry-specific certifications when required. More resources for injection molding Learn more about how injection molding works and how to design the best parts for this technology. Want to learn more about injection molding? Injection molding guide What are the common applications of injection molding and its top benefits? How to avoid common defects in injection molding What’s the best SPI surface finish for your injection molded part? How do you design parts for injection molding? What is injection molding? Why is draft angle design essential for injection molding? FAQ's about injection molding service How much does plastic injection molding cost? There are many factors that determine the cost of injection molding your custom parts. The three main expenses are tooling, materials and production. Find out how to reduce your manufacturing costs in our injection molding guide . Who owns the injection mold? Customers retain ownership of all custom tooling they develop, however, any reusable proprietary components developed by the manufacturing partner (MP) will become the MP’s property. All custom tooling will remain at the MP’s facility for a minimum of two years unless otherwise agreed. If the tooling is inactive after two years, the MP may contact Protolabs Network to determine if the tool must be retained for additional time. Protolabs Network will then contact the customer to make further arrangements. Molds can be transferred to any desired location upon request and at the requester's expense. What happens if an injection molding partner leaves our network? Whenever a manufacturing partner leaves our network, we carry the cost of transferring all molds to another MP in the network, ensuring that your parts get delivered on time. What is the available capacity/timeline for reorders? In general, we have the RFQ ready within 24 hours. It takes two days to set up the mold and order and process the materials, and one day for packing and sending the order out to be shipped. The volume of your parts will determine the number of days required for manufacturing. What ISO certifications do you have? Our injection molding manufacturing network includes partners certified to ISO 9001 for quality management, with additional certifications available for specialized applications. These include IATF 16949 for automotive manufacturing, ISO 13485 for medical devices, and ISO 14001 for environmental management. ISO Class 8 cleanroom capabilities are also available for qualifying projects. Certification availability varies by manufacturing partner and project requirements. Contact us or upload your CAD files to confirm the appropriate certified manufacturing option for your application. How long do you store my mold for? Your injection molding mold is kept at our manufacturing partner facilities for reuse for a minimum of 2 years. If you would like to reorder from your mold, please contact your account manager or networksales@protolabs.com . What is the maximum part size for injection molding? The maximum part size depends on the part geometry, material, mold design, and required machine tonnage. Our manufacturing network can accommodate molds up to 2,000 × 1,800 × 600 mm , supporting both small precision components and large molded parts. Upload your CAD file to confirm the appropriate mold size, machine tonnage, and manufacturing approach for your design. What injection molding machine tonnage is available? Our manufacturing network offers injection molding machines ranging from 35 to 1,300 tons , supporting everything from small precision components to large molded parts. The required tonnage depends on factors such as part size, material, geometry, and projected area. Upload your CAD file, and we'll determine the appropriate machine for your project. What materials are available for plastic injection molding? Our manufacturing network supports a wide range of thermoplastics, including ABS, PC, PP, PA (including 10–50% glass-filled grades), POM, TPU, TPE, HDPE, LDPE, PMMA, PBT, HIPS, PPS, PEEK, PEI (Ultem), PET, LCP, and PC/ABS , as well as LSR (liquid silicone rubber) . Specialty options include food-grade and medical-grade materials, recycled and bio-based polymers, electrically conductive plastics, UL94 V-0 flame-retardant grades, and UV-stable materials . Customer-supplied materials can also be accommodated for suitable projects. Material availability and grade requirements vary by project, so contact us or upload your CAD files to confirm the best material for your application. What quality assurance and inspection options are available for injection molding? Our injection molding network supports a range of quality assurance, inspection, and production validation requirements. Depending on your project and manufacturing partner, available services include PPAP Level 2 and Level 3, First Article Inspection (FAI), CMM inspection, process capability analysis (Cpk), Gauge R&R (GR&R), and Installation/Operational/Performance Qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) . For projects with specific regulatory or compliance requirements, California Proposition 65 (Prop 65) support is also available. Quality documentation and inspection requirements should be specified when requesting a quote so we can match your project with an appropriately qualified manufacturing partner. Learn more Insert molding A manufacturing process in which a part is molded around a pre-installed insert in the tooling. Overmolding A manufacturing process in which one plastic material is molded over another to create a single component. Liquid silicone rubber molding A thermoset process that involves mixing a two-part solution together to produce flexible and durable parts. Find out more about the timeline. Download our Gantt chart. You can specify which secondary operations are needed in the “custom requirements” part of your quote request. SPI surface finishes We offer any type of SPI surface finish, such as A-1, D-2 or D-3. Find the right SPI finish for your part VDI surface finishes We offer any type of VDI surface finish, such as VDI28, VDI30 or VDI 33. Looking for Mold-Tech (MT) or Yick Sang (YS) textures? We support both texture standards, along with custom surface finishes. Upload your CAD Injection molding materials Choose from a wide range of standard, engineering, and specialty materials. Additional grades are available on request. Reorder as required You can easily reorder parts by contacting your account manager The Protolabs Network Standard - consistent quality, every time Protolabs Network applies a rigorous set of standards to every custom part, ensuring quality and consistency for injection molded components. We inspect each order dimensionally and visually during and after production. Tolerances & dimensional accuracy Tolerances & dimensional accuracy Learn more Mold finish standards Mold finish standards Learn more Quality control procedures Quality control procedures Learn more Certifications Our manufacturing network includes ISO 9001-certified partners, with IATF 16949, ISO 13485, ISO 14001, and ISO Class 8 cleanroom capabilities available for qualifying projects. Inspection & quality documentation Advanced inspection and quality documentation are available on request, including PPAP, FAI, CMM inspection, Cpk analysis, GR&R, and IQ/OQ/PQ for qualifying projects. Read more about The Protolabs Network Standard Our injection molding team Manufacturing doesn’t have to be an anonymous process. We have a dedicated team of injection molding project engineers and support staff on the ground to help make sure everything runs smoothly and on time, every time. "I take care of your parts from start to finish, making sure you receive the parts on time and exactly as you requested.” Shak Akharov, Injection Molding Technical Program Manager “I guarantee that your parts go through an extensive quality control process, so they will always be up to spec.” Wilmer Milloria, Quality Control Manager “I make sure we always have a manufacturing partner in our network that fits your manufacturing needs. ” Ruiqi Li, Supply Chain Manager “I ensure our customers are constantly updated on the status of the project and guarantee that they experience a smooth ordering process.” Carlos Blasco, Injection Molding Application Engineer What are the customer experiences of our injection molding service? "It was really helpful to have someone to spar with and test out new ideas on the platform, get a new price for them, and ultimately go into production.” Otect “Having someone who can be in touch with the manufacturers was essential for us.” LEKTRI.CO “You can just upload the parts and get a quote directly. It was just awesome”. Zinstax The advantages of injection molding with us Variety of materials Injection molding offers vast flexibility in material selection. Depending on the mechanical properties your parts require, you can achieve impact- and chemical-resistance, rubber-like elasticity and dimensional stability with molded parts. Our experts can help to manufacture molded parts that are optimized to perform in industrial applications, including parts designed for aerospace, automotive and consumer electronics. We can source thousands of custom materials on request and can advise you on the best choice for your project while minimizing your costs along the way. Single, multi-cavity, and family molds No matter the scale of your injection molding project, we can help you to design and build the ideal tooling and mold for cost-efficient production. As well as single molds, we can advise on multi-cavity molds that simultaneously produce multiple identical models – reducing your cost per part and speeding up production. Our manufacturing partners also work with family molds that optimize tooling costs by producing different parts within the same mold. This is ideal for parts or products that have multiple components of the same material but with different geometries. High quality standards The injection molding process results in finely tuned parts that are highly accurate and consistent. Protolabs Network guarantees the quality of every part that flows through our manufacturing partner network. Our comprehensive quality management processes ensure your molded parts are always up to spec, and that we only work with thoroughly vetted suppliers. We offer various types of quality documentation and can match your project with a manufacturing partner that has industry-specific certifications when required. More resources for injection molding Learn more about how injection molding works and how to design the best parts for this technology. Want to learn more about injection molding? Injection molding guide What are the common applications of injection molding and its top benefits? How to avoid common defects in injection molding What’s the best SPI surface finish for your injection molded part? How do you design parts for injection molding? What is injection molding? Why is draft angle design essential for injection molding? FAQ's about injection molding service How much does plastic injection molding cost? There are many factors that determine the cost of injection molding your custom parts. The three main expenses are tooling, materials and production. Find out how to reduce your manufacturing costs in our injection molding guide . Who owns the injection mold? Customers retain ownership of all custom tooling they develop, however, any reusable proprietary components developed by the manufacturing partner (MP) will become the MP’s property. All custom tooling will remain at the MP’s facility for a minimum of two years unless otherwise agreed. If the tooling is inactive after two years, the MP may contact Protolabs Network to determine if the tool must be retained for additional time. Protolabs Network will then contact the customer to make further arrangements. Molds can be transferred to any desired location upon request and at the requester's expense. What happens if an injection molding partner leaves our network? Whenever a manufacturing partner leaves our network, we carry the cost of transferring all molds to another MP in the network, ensuring that your parts get delivered on time. What is the available capacity/timeline for reorders? In general, we have the RFQ ready within 24 hours. It takes two days to set up the mold and order and process the materials, and one day for packing and sending the order out to be shipped. The volume of your parts will determine the number of days required for manufacturing. What ISO certifications do you have? Our injection molding manufacturing network includes partners certified to ISO 9001 for quality management, with additional certifications available for specialized applications. These include IATF 16949 for automotive manufacturing, ISO 13485 for medical devices, and ISO 14001 for environmental management. ISO Class 8 cleanroom capabilities are also available for qualifying projects. Certification availability varies by manufacturing partner and project requirements. Contact us or upload your CAD files to confirm the appropriate certified manufacturing option for your application. How long do you store my mold for? Your injection molding mold is kept at our manufacturing partner facilities for reuse for a minimum of 2 years. If you would like to reorder from your mold, please contact your account manager or networksales@protolabs.com . What is the maximum part size for injection molding? The maximum part size depends on the part geometry, material, mold design, and required machine tonnage. Our manufacturing network can accommodate molds up to 2,000 × 1,800 × 600 mm , supporting both small precision components and large molded parts. Upload your CAD file to confirm the appropriate mold size, machine tonnage, and manufacturing approach for your design. What injection molding machine tonnage is available? Our manufacturing network offers injection molding machines ranging from 35 to 1,300 tons , supporting everything from small precision components to large molded parts. The required tonnage depends on factors such as part size, material, geometry, and projected area. Upload your CAD file, and we'll determine the appropriate machine for your project. What materials are available for plastic injection molding? Our manufacturing network supports a wide range of thermoplastics, including ABS, PC, PP, PA (including 10–50% glass-filled grades), POM, TPU, TPE, HDPE, LDPE, PMMA, PBT, HIPS, PPS, PEEK, PEI (Ultem), PET, LCP, and PC/ABS , as well as LSR (liquid silicone rubber) . Specialty options include food-grade and medical-grade materials, recycled and bio-based polymers, electrically conductive plastics, UL94 V-0 flame-retardant grades, and UV-stable materials . Customer-supplied materials can also be accommodated for suitable projects. Material availability and grade requirements vary by project, so contact us or upload your CAD files to confirm the best material for your application. What quality assurance and inspection options are available for injection molding? Our injection molding network supports a range of quality assurance, inspection, and production validation requirements. Depending on your project and manufacturing partner, available services include PPAP Level 2 and Level 3, First Article Inspection (FAI), CMM inspection, process capability analysis (Cpk), Gauge R&R (GR&R), and Installation/Operational/Performance Qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) . For projects with specific regulatory or compliance requirements, California Proposition 65 (Prop 65) support is also available. Quality documentation and inspection requirements should be specified when requesting a quote so we can match your project with an appropriately qualified manufacturing partner. Published Jul 29, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility.
